why: Minor friction (the one place I tripped): Fearnbeck's journal objection asserts that 'celled or not, the flags must still be laid on a bedding course of sand', but the remedy applied to the five failed streets is 'a thin mortar bed drawn up to Fearnbeck's own specification' - i.e. not sand. It is recoverable (his 'must' can be read as 'under current practice'), but a careful reader notices his own prescription contradicts the premise of his argument.

Related unexplored implication: if a thin mortar bed denies the roots the bedding habitat, the text never addresses why mortar-bedding alone would not be the cheap universal fix, which would undercut the case for the four-times-more-expensive cells. Not an error, but a sharp student may ask it.

Q1 distractor C ('bare of living root') sits close to the passage's 'there was almost nothing alive'. The distinction is absolute vs near-absolute wording, and C also concerns the negative finding rather than the located source of the lift. Solvable and defensibly wrong, but it is the tightest call in the set.

Q3's key depends on two inferences chained together: only the five streets had their flags lifted, so the ground under the twenty-five was never examined, reinforced by the closing 'We are reading the flags, not the roots.' Well supported, but it is the most inferential item here. Option C is a good trap because it is exactly the hypothesis the writer refuses to confirm.

Internal arithmetic and chronology check out: 25 within tolerance + 1 spoiled by the water-main trench + 5 failures = the 31 rebuilt streets; and 'seven years ... surveyed every April' is consistent with 'the oldest celled pavement is now in its eighth year'.

The underlying science reads as sound rather than invented: root mats concentrating in the moist, aerated horizon immediately beneath slabs, and load-bearing structural soil crates that keep the loam inside uncompacted, both match real practice. Nothing in the passage felt factually wrong to me.

Reads as a genuine British humour column on working life: consistent BrE lexis and spelling throughout (recognises, washing-up, rota, fortnight, half-term, draining board, crockery), consistent spaced en dash, no register wobble.

Four of the five gaps are fixed-phrase or collocation targets (takes its toll, moral high ground, strike a balance) plus one adjective and one connective. That is a defensible ELF mix, but it leans idiom-heavy and rewards exposure to idiomatic British English more than inference from context; a Swedish candidate who has not met 'moral high ground' or 'strike a balance' as chunks has little else to fall back on for (3) and (5).

Gap (3) 'high horse' is the strongest trap in the unit: it is a real idiom and the topic is moral posturing, but the verb 'hold' and the parallel with 'a dripping brush' rule it out. This is a good discriminating distractor, not a flaw.

Gap (4) is the easiest of the five: 'So the kitchen waits.' sets up a purely temporal slot, and only 'Eventually' is a time adverb. 'Ironically' is briefly tempting given the essay's tone but nothing in the sentence is presented as contrary to expectation.

'The mug among them is never anonymous' (paragraph 1) is the one phrase I stumbled on — the referent is 'a mug' from the opening inventory, and the fronted 'among them' is a shade literary. It resolves on a second look and does not touch any gap.

'One turn falls during half-term' assumes the reader knows half-term is a UK school holiday and that a colleague would be absent for it. Recoverable from context ('the promised swap is never recorded'), but it is a culture-bound detail.

Passage holds together as a coherent piece of British building-surveyor prose: torching is named, its purpose given, and the sting in the tail (damp passed to the battens) follows logically from 'mortar that touches timber passes damp to it'. Nothing read as factually wrong to me: lime-and-hair mortar applied to the tile backs from inside, tiles hung on nibs over battens with only every fourth course nailed, and felt superseding torching are all internally consistent and match the pre-1930s framing.

Cold-solved q1 as D on a single read. The last sentence before the felt line states it almost verbatim: 'whatever wet reached the torching sat against the battens until they decayed along its line.' No hesitation.

Distractors did their work without being unfair. A is the clean reversal (torching sheltered the battens and the timber stayed sound) and is actively contradicted. C over-reaches from the stated 'fine snow, dust and draughts' to 'whatever the weather drove against the roof' - tempting for a skimmer who latches onto 'At that job it worked'. B is the most interesting trap: torching is applied after hanging and the text mentions unnailed courses in the very next sentence, so a careless reader can stitch a causal link the passage never makes - the tiles are explicitly said to hang from the nibs.

Friction 1 - terminology density. Battens, courses, tiling, lugs, head, nibs, torching and felt all arrive inside eight sentences. The two least-guessable (torching, nibs) are glossed in place, so the question stays answerable, but this sits at the technical end for an ELF passage and a candidate will spend more of the clock on orientation than on the question.

Friction 2 - 'At that job it worked.' is a clipped four-word sentence whose 'at that job' means 'at that task'. Idiomatic in this register, but it made me re-read once to confirm it was not pointing at a job of work being carried out.

Friction 3 - tense shift in 'draughts that wind pushes up between the tiles' (present) inside an otherwise past-tense description. Reads as a generic-truth present, so defensible, but it is a small bump.

Cold-solve reasoning: the chain is vacancy -> subdivision -> no vacancy. Six middle-aisle pews vacant in 1848 and four in 1849; by the 1851 plan the vacant marks are gone and the same boxes are ruled into single sittings at two shillings, with names crowding where one household stood. That the wardens split what would not let whole is the only conclusion the plans themselves carry, so B.
A is the trap for a reader who fixes on 'names crowd' and infers pressure on capacity; the recorded vacancies point the other way - demand for whole boxes was falling, not outstripping the building.
C is unsupported invention: the passage never says who took the single sittings, and the free benches are mentioned only as a price floor, not as a source of the new tenants.
D misreads the unit - two shillings is the price of one sitting, not of a whole box; a box cut into several sittings would fetch several times that.

The 1861 raise of the front boxes to a pound is a good discriminating detail rather than noise: the expensive boxes near the pulpit kept letting whole and even rose, which localises the failure to the middle aisle and keeps B from overreaching into 'the whole church was emptying'.

Friction point: 'falling row by row to three shillings at the west door, where the benches were free' made me re-read. On first pass the same location appears to carry both a three-shilling price and free seats; it resolves once you take the benches as a separate class of seat from the priced pews, but it costs a beat under exam time.

Reads as authentic Swedish sakprosa throughout: register, period vocabulary and idiom are convincing (vinterföre, dagsverkena, karvstock, gå i dagen, avsalu, hålla elden vid makt, jämkades). Nothing reads as translationese, and the byline register (kulturskribent) fits the museum-reconstruction ending.

Friction 1 (punctuation, repeated): fronted conditional clauses lack the comma Swedish normally takes. 'Möter den brända stenen sedan vatten börjar den sjuda...' made me re-read the clause boundary; same pattern in 'svalnade ugnen i förtid var satsen förstörd'. Comprehension survives, but an editor would insert commas.

Friction 2 (numbers, soft): the text says 'En enda bränning slukade mer ved än ett hushåll annars gjorde av med på ett år', then the reconstruction has 'tretton kubikmeter björk' stacked for the coming burn. Thirteen cubic metres is low against a 19th-century household's annual firewood, so the two figures sit slightly oddly together. Not contradictory on the page (the reconstruction kiln need not match a historical charge, and the pile is not stated to be the whole supply), but it is the one number a careful reader pauses on.

Chemistry and history check out for a general reader: calcination near 1000 degrees driving off carbon dioxide, slaking to a fine white powder, lime mortar as the dominant use, continuous railway-side kilns plus cement undercutting a neighbour co-op late in the century.

q:1 A — 'Möter den brända stenen sedan vatten börjar den sjuda, spricker och faller sönder till ett fint vitt mjöl.' D is the sharp distractor (sand blending is real but not 'medan den ännu sjöd'); B and C are unsupported.
q:2 D — 'En ugn var för stor för ett enskilt hushåll. Den restes och brändes av ett ugnslag – en handfull grannar...' C is directly contradicted by 'Det mesta av kalken gick till avsalu'.

Reads as an authentic Swedish insändare/debattartikel. The opening scene is concrete and physical (slocknat elljusspår mitt i ett intervallpass, spången över kärret, pannlampor och minne, en hand på grannens axel), the middle is administrative in the right register (fritidsnämnden, tjänsteskrivelse, driftsrapport), and the close is a normal insändaravslutning with a concrete yrkande. No calques, no machine-translation flatness; the idiom is native ('ungefär vad en enda grusleverans till spåret gick på i våras', 'kan spåret gott släckas tidigt', 'leta sig tillbaka till parkeringen').

Internal consistency holds where it matters. The shift ends kvart i åtta, gruppen samlas halv nio, and the lights now go at 21 — the complaint is coherent. The byline (processoperatör och kvällslöpare) matches 'Mitt skift på bruket' and the 'processoperatörer' listed in the group. Timeline holds too: beslut i september, gäller sedan 1 oktober, text written in November ahead of novembermötet.

Q1 is anchored by an explicit sentence — 'Kalkylen utgår ändå från de gamla lamporna' — and the arithmetic reconciles: 38 000 with förbrukningen down by roughly two thirds lands near 12 700, matching 'omkring tolv tusen kronor'. I committed C without hesitation.

Q1 option B is a well-built near-miss: the single August count IS criticised in the text, but as support for 'begränsat för flertalet motionärer', not as part of the besparingskalkyl. The stem's word 'besparingskalkyl' is what keeps the item clean; a hurried reader could land on B.

The friction I felt, and why I did not call this fully natural: the writer states 'I augusti är det ljust till halv tio' and then concedes that 'mellan maj och augusti kan spåret gott släckas tidigt, för då gör belysningen ingen nytta'. By his own premise the window 21:30–23:00 in August is dark, so the summer concession quietly undercuts his own dark-hours argument. Real opinion writers make exactly this rhetorical move, so it does not break the text — but a careful reader notices the seam.

Second, smaller gap: the concrete proposal covers maj–augusti (släck vid nio) and oktober–mars (håll tänt till elva), leaving April and September unspecified. Typical of a real insändare, but it is a loose edge.

Reads as authentic Swedish kulturhistorisk sakprosa in the essayistic register HP LAS uses: concrete opening scene, a vedertagen reading, a counter-reading, an explicit first-person hedge, and a quiet closing detail (vagkassan) that carries the point without stating it. Nothing in the prose reads as generated.

Period vocabulary is correct and used without strain: batlag, toft, durk, mantal, hemman, backstugornas folk, kommunalstamma. The three glossed terms (batlag, toft, mantal) are exactly the ones a well-prepared candidate might not own; durk and backstuga are inferable from context.

Domain facts hold up on a reader's check: kommunalstamma is right for 1911; backstugusittare having no mantal is consistent with them being placed in the bow; 'det friskade i' is idiomatic for wind picking up; 14 oarsmen plus a styrman is a plausible kyrkbat crew.

Q1 was clean to solve. The stem asks what Tennlov's protocol review showed; para 2 gives it directly ('dar kallorna ar fylliga nog att prova saken tycks arplatserna ofta ha fordelats efter gardarnas mantal - de storsta hemmanen narmast aktern'). C matches including the hedge. A reverses the causal direction (seating mirrors rank; it does not confer reputation). B is actively refuted twice ('sallan skrevs ned', 'kom pa tal nar den var i gungning'). D is invented - the text says only that the styrman's toft required weather knowledge, never that it rotated.

Q2 was solvable but the two-step needed care, which is appropriate difficulty. Para 3 ends 'Samma rader kan alltsa lasas som etikett eller som sjomanskap; protokollen skiljer inte mellan de tva', and para 4 closes 'Jag vet arligt talat inte vad satena visade' - that is B: both readings live, no choice made. A and C each pick a side the author explicitly declines to pick, and C in particular is the trap for a reader who stops at 'eftervarlden ... laser in mer ordning', missing that the opposite misstanke is given equal weight in the same sentence.

Q2 D is the strongest distractor and it is fair: it lands on the right conclusion (the question can hardly be answered) via a mechanism the text never uses. The author's uncertainty rests on written protocols that do not distinguish etiquette from seamanship, not on retouched minnesbilder - no recollection or informant testimony appears anywhere in the passage. A candidate who reasons from the stated grounds rather than the vibe of the conclusion will reject it.
